steps: Find the time signature. The top number is how many beats fill a bar.
Is the top number 2, 3 or 4 (simple) or 6, 9 or 12 (compound)?
For each note, check the head first, then count the tails.
Look for dots. A dot adds half of that note's own value.
method_card.title: Reading how long a note lasts
method_card.content:
In Lesson 1 you followed a line while it played. Now put names to the lengths you were already hearing.

Then the metre: how the beats themselves are grouped and divided.

options: Bar 1 — the notes are played too fast
Bar 2 — the first note is lengthened and the second shortened
Bar 3 — the last note is too short
Bar 2 — a note is missing altogether
gold.question: Play Extract D. The pitches are all correct, but one bar is not played as printed. Which one, and what changed?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as four even crotchets. What sounds is a long-short pair followed by two even notes — the first note borrows half a beat from the second, giving the dotted, lopsided feel. The bar still totals four beats, which is exactly why this is easy to miss unless you are reading along.

options: They cannot — six quavers always sound the same
3/4 groups them as three pairs, 6/8 as two threes
3/4 is simple because it uses crotchets and 6/8 is compound because it uses quavers
gold.question: Why can a piece in 3/4 and a piece in 6/8 both have six quavers in a bar, yet feel completely different?
gold.explanation: Same six quavers, different grouping. 3/4 is three crotchet beats each splitting in two; 6/8 is two dotted-crotchet beats each splitting in three. The beaming on the page shows you which, and the accent pattern lets you hear it.

gold.question: Play Extract E. One bar is not played with the printed rhythm. Which?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as four crotchets. What sounds is crotchet, minim, crotchet — the second note takes the third note's beat. The bar still lasts four beats, so only reading along reveals it.

gold.question: Play Extract F. One bar is not played in even threes. Which?
gold.explanation: 6/8 gives two beats, each splitting into three EVEN quavers. Bar 2 is played long-short, long-short — a lopsided swing the page does not ask for. The beaming still shows even groups of three, so the performance and the notation disagree.

gold.question: Play Extract G. One dotted note is not held for its printed length. Which bar?
gold.explanation: Every bar is printed as a dotted minim (3 beats) plus a crotchet. In bar 2 the first note is held for only two beats and the second stretches to two, so the dotted long-short shape becomes two equal halves and the dot is effectively ignored.

bronze.question: A note has a hollow head and a stem, and no tail. How long is it?
bronze.explanation: That is a minim: 2 beats. Hollow means long, and the stem — the plain vertical line — never changes the length. Only a semibreve, which has no stem at all, is longer.

bronze.question: Play Extract B. How many beats does the first note last?
bronze.explanation: A hollow head with a dot: the minim is 2 beats and the dot adds half of 2, making 3. Tap the beat while it plays and you will feel it hold for three.

bronze.question: A piece has a 6/8 time signature. Is it simple or compound time?
bronze.explanation: The TOP number decides it: 6, 9 or 12 means compound, so each beat divides into three. The bottom number only tells you which note gets the beat.

bronze.question: Play Extract H. Which note lasts longest, and how many beats?
bronze.explanation: The last note is hollow with a stem — a minim, 2 beats — while the first two are filled crotchets of 1 beat each. Together they fill the four-beat bar.

silver.question: Play Extract A. How many beats are in each bar?
silver.explanation: The time signature reads 3 over 4 — three crotchet beats per bar. Count the highlight: it moves three times before the bar line each time.

options: Into two, so it is simple time
Into three, so it is compound time
Into four, so it is simple time
silver.question: Play Extract C. How do the beats divide?
silver.explanation: You can hear the quavers grouping in threes, and see them beamed in threes on the page. 6/8 is compound duple: two beats a bar, each a dotted crotchet worth three quavers.

silver.question: A dotted crotchet lasts how long?
silver.explanation: A crotchet is 1 beat and the dot adds half of 1. The rule is always 'half of the note's own value' — which is why the same dot makes a minim 3 but a crotchet 1½.

options: Four — there are four notes in bar 2
Three — the time signature reads 3 over 4, and each bar totals three beats
Two — the first bar has two notes
silver.question: Play Extract I. How many beats are in each bar, and how do you know?
silver.explanation: The top number of the time signature gives the beats per bar. Bar 1 is a minim plus a crotchet (2 + 1) and bar 2 is three crotchets — both total three.

steps.label: Step 1 — read the head
steps.content: It is hollow, so it is at least a minim: 2 beats.

steps.label: Step 2 — check for a dot
steps.content: There is a dot after it. A dot adds half the note's own value, and half of 2 is 1.

steps.label: Step 3 — confirm by ear
steps.content: Play it and tap the beat. The first note holds for three taps before the next one arrives.

steps: Scan below the stave for letters — those are dynamics.
Look above and below the note heads for dots (staccato) and curved lines (slurs).
Check the clef at the start of each stave before you read any pitch.
In a full score, read top to bottom: woodwind, brass, percussion, strings.
method_card.title: Reading expression and forces

gold.question: Play Extract F. The articulation is played correctly, but one printed note is not the pitch you hear. Where?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as a stepwise climb G, A, B, C. On the third beat you hear the top C arrive a beat early, so the printed B never sounds and the note repeats instead. The staccato bar before it is played exactly as written, which is what makes this one harder to locate.

options: It starts quietly and gets louder, and sounds quite smooth
It begins p and changes to f at bar 3; the notes are unmarked, so they are played normally rather than staccato or slurred
gold.question: A Section A question shows you this extract and asks you to 'describe the dynamics and articulation'. Which answer would score best?
gold.explanation: The strongest answer names the marking, translates it, and says WHERE it happens. A bare list of terms shows recognition but not reading; a vague impression shows neither.

gold.question: Play Extract G. One printed articulation is not what you hear. Which bar?
gold.explanation: Bar 3 is printed with staccato dots but is played smoothly and joined, with no gaps between the notes. Bars 1 and 2 are played exactly as marked, so the contrast you can hear between them is correct and only the third bar disagrees with the page.

gold.question: Play Extract H. The dynamics are played correctly. One pitch is not. Where?
gold.explanation: Bar 2 is printed as a stepwise climb G, A, B, C. The last beat sounds above the printed C, so the loud bar overshoots. The dynamic change at bar 2 is played exactly as written, which draws the ear away from the wrong note.

gold.question: Play Extract I. The articulation is right throughout, but one note is not the printed length. Where?
gold.explanation: The last bar is printed as a semibreve — four beats. It sounds for two and then stops, so the extract ends early. Checking that a final long note actually lasts its full value is easy to forget once the interesting material has gone past.

bronze.question: What does the marking mf mean?
bronze.explanation: mf is mezzo-forte: moderately loud. The ladder runs pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff — 'mezzo' means moderately, and it softens whichever word follows it.

options: Hold it for half as long again
bronze.question: A dot is printed above a note head. What does it tell the player?
bronze.explanation: A dot above or below the head means staccato: short and detached. Do not confuse it with a dot AFTER the head, which lengthens the note by half its value.

bronze.question: Play the longer extract. What dynamic does it begin with?
bronze.explanation: There is a p below the stave at the start, so it begins quiet. The f at bar 3 marks where it changes.

options: p then f — quiet, then loud
f then p — loud, then quiet
bronze.question: Look at Extract J. Which two dynamic markings appear, and in which order?
bronze.explanation: The f sits below the first note and the p below the last bar. A dynamic mark applies from where it appears until the next one changes it, so this extract begins loud and drops to quiet.

silver.question: In the longer extract, where does the dynamic change and what to?
silver.explanation: The f appears at the start of bar 3 and applies from there onward. A dynamic mark holds until the next one, so bars 1-2 are quiet and bars 3-5 loud.

options: The curve means play them smoothly joined; the dot means play that note short
The curve means repeat; the dot means louder
The curve means slow down; the dot means speed up
silver.question: What is the difference between a curved line over several different notes and a dot above one note?
silver.explanation: A slur asks for legato — smooth and connected. A staccato dot asks for the opposite: short, with a gap after it. They are often contrasted deliberately within one phrase.

options: The lines represent lower pitches, so a lower instrument or the left hand
The music has no key signature
silver.question: A stave begins with a bass clef. What does that tell you?
silver.explanation: The clef redefines what the five lines mean. Bass clef indicates lower-sounding parts — cello, bassoon, or a pianist's left hand. Always read the clef before any pitch.

options: Bar 1 is short and detached (staccato); bar 2 is smooth and joined (legato)
silver.question: Play Extract K. How does bar 2 differ from bar 1 in the way the notes are played?
silver.explanation: The dots above bar 1 mean staccato, so each note stops early and leaves a gap. The curved line over bar 2 is a slur, asking for legato — the notes run into one another.

steps.label: Step 1 — find the letters
steps.content: There is a p at the very start and an f at the beginning of bar 3.

steps.label: Step 2 — translate them
steps.content: p is piano, quiet. f is forte, loud.

steps.label: Step 3 — say where
steps.content: A mark applies from where it appears until the next one. So bars 1-2 are quiet and bars 3-5 are loud.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: It begins quietly (p) and becomes loud (f) at bar 3. Naming the marking AND the bar is what earns the mark.
